title: One shard is getting way more traffic than the others — what do you do?
summary: The applied hot-partition question. Learn to tell a hot key from a hot shard before proposing virtual shards, a split, or a resharding project.

slides.markdown:
This question drops you into an already-broken system and checks whether you diagnose before you fix. "One shard is hot" has at least two different causes — a single overloaded row (a hot key) or a badly chosen distribution across the whole shard (a hot shard) — and each has a different, cheaper-or-more-expensive fix.

A weak answer jumps straight to "reshard everything." A strong one diagnoses which problem this actually is first, since the fix for one can be useless or wasteful for the other.

Ask: **is the whole shard hot, or is one key on it hot?** Check whether traffic to that shard is concentrated on a single row or ID, or spread evenly across everything the shard holds. These look identical from the outside ("this shard's QPS is 5x the others") but need opposite fixes.

Also ask: is the traffic evenly spread but simply landing on too few shards overall — meaning the real issue isn't skew at all, just under-provisioning? Ruling this out first avoids solving a problem that doesn't exist.

Structure it as: **diagnose which of the three it is, then apply the matching fix.** Hot key on one shard → isolate that key onto dedicated capacity. Hot shard from bad key distribution → split the shard or add virtual shards to spread it. Evenly spread load on too few shards → add capacity, no redesign needed.

Naming this three-way branch up front, before committing to a fix, is what distinguishes a diagnosed answer from a guessed one.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: virtual shards to spread a hot range cheaply
slides.markdown:
When the problem is a badly distributed shard, **virtual (or consistent) hashing** lets you spread its data across more physical nodes without a full resharding project. Instead of mapping keys directly to N physical shards, you map keys to many more virtual shards (say, 1000), then assign multiple virtual shards to each physical node.

Rebalancing now means moving a handful of virtual shards to a new or underloaded physical node — a targeted, cheap operation — instead of re-hashing and moving the entire dataset.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: splitting a shard for one viral group
slides.markdown:
For a genuine hot-key case, say a single viral group's data lives on a shard alongside many normal groups and now dominates its traffic — the direct fix is giving that one group **its own dedicated shard**, pulled out of the shared pool. Every other group on the original shard is unaffected and stays put.

This is deliberately narrow: you're not resharding the dataset, you're carving out capacity for one specific hot value while leaving the general layout untouched.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: confirming it's really one hot shard
slides.markdown:
Before fixing anything, confirm the diagnosis with per-shard metrics:

```
shard-01: 1,200 QPS
shard-02: 1,150 QPS
shard-03: 9,800 QPS   <- hot
shard-04: 1,300 QPS
```

Then drill into shard-03's key-level breakdown to see if it's one key or evenly spread:

```
key "group_88231": 8,900 QPS   <- the hot key
(all other keys on this shard): ~900 QPS combined
```

This single check tells you whether to isolate one key or redesign the shard's whole distribution — skip it and you risk fixing the wrong problem.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this explicitly: **virtual shards fix distribution cheaply but add a lookup indirection to every single request** — one more hop (key → virtual shard → physical node) that has to be right on every read and write, forever.

That indirection is a permanent architectural cost paid on every request, not a one-time migration cost. It's usually worth it, but naming it — rather than presenting virtual shards as a free win — is what a senior answer sounds like.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the hot shard is hot because of a celebrity account
slides.markdown:
Resharding the whole dataset doesn't help here — the celebrity account's traffic would simply become hot on whatever new shard it lands on, since the underlying imbalance is about one value's traffic volume, not the layout. The fix is the same isolate-the-key move: give that one account dedicated capacity, possibly with extra caching in front of it since celebrity data is also disproportionately read.

Say this explicitly — resharding is the wrong tool for a hot-key problem no matter how the shards are laid out.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: detecting a hot shard before it pages someone
slides.markdown:
Name concrete monitoring, not "we'd have alerts." Track per-shard QPS and per-shard latency with alerting on relative deviation — a shard running 3-5x the median across its peers, not just an absolute threshold that might be normal for peak traffic overall.

For proactive detection, periodically sample key-level traffic distribution on each shard, not just aggregate QPS, so a hot key building up gets caught while it's still a minor imbalance rather than after it's already saturating the shard.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: resharding everything for a one-key problem
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "One shard is hot — let's reshard the whole dataset to a new layout."

**Why it's wrong:** if the real cause is one hot key (a viral post, a celebrity account), resharding moves that same hot key to a different shard under the new layout — the imbalance follows the key, not the layout. You've paid the cost of a full migration and the same shard is still hot.

**Correct model:** diagnose hot-key vs hot-shard first. A hot key gets isolated onto dedicated capacity; only a genuinely bad distribution across many keys justifies a resharding project.

"I'd check per-shard metrics first to see whether this is one hot key, a badly distributed shard, or just even load on too few shards. A hot key — a viral group, a celebrity account — gets isolated onto its own dedicated capacity; resharding wouldn't help since the imbalance follows the key. A genuinely hot shard from poor distribution gets fixed with virtual shards, spreading it across more physical nodes at the cost of one extra lookup hop per request. I wouldn't reshard the whole dataset until I've ruled out the cheaper, targeted fixes."
